title: Fast Nondestructive Readout for High-Clock-Rate Atom Array Quantum Processor
authors: Xu-Zhao-Qiu Zeng, Chang You, Qing-Wei Wang, Zi-Feng Li, Yi Ji, Dong An, Chao Yu, Jia-Rui Liu, Zi-Mo He, Jia-Rui Gu, Yuhao Mei, Hao-Wen Cheng, Yu-Chen Zhang, Rui Lin, Zhan Wu, Jun Rui, Jun Zhang, Ming-Cheng Chen, Yu-Hao Deng, Chao-Yang Lu, Jian-Wei Pan
abstract: Neutral-atom arrays have rapidly advanced to support thousands of qubits and execute high-fidelity logical operations. However, these processors remain severely throttled by their slowest fundamental operation: nondestructive qubit measurement, which requires milliseconds and fundamentally limits the system's clock rate. This bottleneck arises from both an inherent photon-budget dilemma---sufficient fluorescence for reliable state discrimination must be collected without excessive heating or loss---and frame-based imaging, which imposes one common exposure and decision latency on intrinsically independent, site-local measurements. Here, we overcome these limitations with a fast, nondestructive readout architecture based on real-time, site-resolved adaptive protection. By integrating continuous photon counting with a dynamic feedforward framework, we decode qubit states with sub-microsecond latency and instantly shield atoms from redundant scattering. Demonstrated in parallel across a 100-qubit reconfigurable atom array, with adaptive protection on a 25-site subarray, this dynamic decision protocol reduces the average probe time to just $15\ μ\text{s}$. Model-free benchmarking yields a discrimination infidelity of $4.1 \times 10^{-5}$ and an atom loss of $2.1 \times 10^{-4}$, simultaneously setting new performance records for atom arrays. Exploiting this capability, we operate repeated quantum circuits at an unprecedented 1.7 kHz clock rate with atoms reused over 120 consecutive rounds---nearly sevenfold higher than the previous record---and enter the sub-millisecond cycle regime for the first time. By removing nondestructive readout as the dominant cycle-time bottleneck, this work unlocks high-clock-rate mid-circuit syndrome extraction, paving the way for high-throughput, fault-tolerant quantum computation.
summary: This paper introduces a novel Fast Nondestructive Readout (FNDR) architecture for neutral-atom quantum processors. By replacing slow, frame-based imaging with a real-time, site-resolved adaptive photon-counting system, they drastically reduce readout latency. This breakthrough enables the operation of quantum circuits at a high clock rate (1.7 kHz), paving the way for scalable, fault-tolerant quantum computation.
main_problem: Nondestructive qubit measurement in neutral-atom arrays is the primary bottleneck, severely limiting the system's clock rate to millisecond timescales.
main_result: The authors developed a fast, nondestructive readout architecture that achieves a sub-microsecond readout latency, enabling repeated quantum circuits at an unprecedented 1.7 kHz clock rate.
method: They implemented a real-time, site-resolved adaptive protection scheme by integrating continuous photon counting with a dynamic feedforward framework.
model_or_system: The experiment uses neutral-atom arrays trapped in optical tweezers, functioning as a quantum processor for qubits. The readout process is fundamentally limited by the need to collect sufficient fluorescence without causing excessive heating or loss.
key_observables: Discrimination infidelity ($4.1 	imes 10^{-5}$), atom loss ($2.1 	imes 10^{-4}$), and the achievable clock rate (1.7 kHz).
important_parameters: Sub-microsecond latency, $15 \mu	ext{s}$ average probe time, and operation in the sub-millisecond cycle regime.
main_assumptions: The method relies on coupling fluorescence into independent photon-counting channels processed by an FPGA to enable rapid, site-local decision-making.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the FNDR architecture, comparing fixed vs. dynamic readout boundaries, and showing time-resolved photon counting profiles demonstrating reduced probe duration.
paper_structure: The paper identifies the measurement bottleneck, proposes the FNDR architecture using continuous photon counting and dynamic feedforward, demonstrates its performance metrics (fidelity, speed), and concludes by showing its application to high-repetition quantum circuit operation.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses the critical engineering bottleneck in scaling quantum processors, moving the system from a measurement-limited regime to one where gate speed and coherence time become the dominant constraints.
